newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST-Iberia bonds may steady if EMU fears fade.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Iberia bonds may steady if EMU fears fade.

text.p: Iberia's bond markets can look forward to a week of consolidation or even slight gains, analysts say, providing there is no fresh outbreak of single currency jitters.

The market will remain cautious but if there are no new statements or developments to question Spain and Portugal's possible membership of monetary union, then investors should concentrate on the generally positive domestic scene, they add.

The downside over the next seven days for the spread with the German 10-year cash bond will be around 150 basis points if the nervousness over economic and monetary union (EMU) persists, from current levels of 129 basis points for Spain and 124 basis points for Portugal.
But a week of relative EMU calm could see the spreads narrowing towards 120 basis points, they add.

"In the (Spanish) bonos and the (Portuguese) OT everybody is very sensitive to statements about EMU. For this reason, the market is going to be very cautious over the next week," said Valentin Fernandez, analyst with Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"With more (negative) statements, the spread between the Bonos (and the Bunds) could go quickly to around 150 basis points," he said.
"Negative opinions about the convergence of the periphery markets could push the (10-year) spreads to 140-160 basis points", said Mario Vigario of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.

Analysts were unanimous that in the short-term, there was good support for the Iberian spreads at 160-170 basis points to the German equivalent which would probably only be broken in the event of talk that the whole project of monetary union was to be delayed beyond its intended 1999 launch.
"Without monetary in 1999, Iberia is left with no reference points for convergence and it would have to pay a higher risk premium," said one trader at a London investment bank.
Assuming no EMU turbulence, the greatest interest in the Iberian market could focus on the shorter end of the yield curve, particularly in Spain, analysts and traders said.

"With an eventual accord on labour (market) reform and a consumer price index (CPI) falling (in February) to 2.8 percent year-on-year, one can think again of the Bank of Spain cutting rates," said Fernandez.
Spain's year-on-year rate was 2.9 percent in January.
"The peseta at 84.30-84.60 (per mark) allows the Spanish repo rate to fall 25 basis points in the short-term," said an analyst at one London bank.
The peseta was at around 84.65 to the mark on Friday morning.
"The Spanish curve could steepen and the spread between the 10 and the two-year cash bonds could widen to 120 basis points (from 115 currently)," said Fernandez.
Analysts said that Portugal might be less buoyant at the short end because its CPI index was only likely to start to ease again from April.

"The Bank of Portugal will probably not cut rates this month. It (a cut) is going to depend on a good CPI, what Spain does and the exchange rate situation," said Isabel Cabral of Lisbon brokers Fincor.
Nevertheless, analysts said that there was little room for spreads to widen between Bonos and the OT at the short end.
The spread between the January 1999 OT and the April 1999 Bono is 19 basis points, compared with zero to five basis points at the end of January.
--Lisbon bureau 3511-3150035
